contributions.headingText: Plasmablastic lymphoma (PBL) is an aggressive lymphoid neoplasm composed of large atypical B cells with plasmablastic or immunoblastic morphology and a terminal B-cell differentiation phenotype, predominantly arising at extranodal sites.

PBL usually involves extranodal sites, such as the nasal/oral cavity (~50%), digestive system (~20%), bone and soft tissues (~15%), and skin (~5%). Nodal involvement can also occur without apparent extranodal disease.

Clinical features of PBL depend on the site involved and the extent of involvement. In the oral cavity, the gingiva and palate are the most commonly affected sites. The tumour induces painful swelling, and features rapid growth with frequent ulceration and necrosis and common bone destruction {20537055; 34091967}. PBL usually arises de novo in patients with immune deficiency/dysregulation {9028965} (see #38978Table 4.42, in section Lymphoid proliferations and lymphomas associated with immune deficiency and dysregulation: Introduction). PBL can also arise secondarily as a transformation of follicular lymphoma or chronic lymphocytic leukaemia / small lymphocytic lymphoma (CLL/SLL) {23282972; 23791008; 26084925}.

PBL is rare, accounting for 1% of large B-cell lymphomas {29019447} and 2% of HIV-related lymphomas {25636338}. There is a male predominance (M:F radio: 3:1) {25636338}. The disease occurs more often in adults than in children {22958176; 25636338}.

The etiology is unknown. PBL occurring in the setting of immune deficiency/dysregulation are generally, but not invariably, associated with EBV. PBL has been reported to occur in the context of newly emerging iatrogenic immune deficiency/dysregulation settings, such as anti-CD19 chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy {26084925}.

Most PBLs occur in the context of immune deficiency/dysregulation (e.g. HIV infection; 31–62%) or immunosuppressive therapy for bone marrow transplant, solid-organ transplantation, or autoimmune diseases (3–7%). PBL may also occur in elderly adults without overt immunodeficiency; in these cases, immunosenescence may contribute to the pathogenesis {24832164; 25636338; 26055271; 27175027; 27687004}. EBV reactivation, with type I and occasionally type II latency, is observed {25636338}. The presence of an EBV abortive lytic cycle profile has been described as a feature {25193957; 33225311}.

Complex karyotypes are common. MYC overexpression is found in as many as 80% of the cases. MYC rearrangements, usually with IG genes, are reported in about 60% of cases {34465776}. Lymphomas with plasmablastic features carrying dual MYC and BCL2 translocations have been exclusively seen in cases transformed from follicular lymphoma {20348882; 19762538; 21088162}. Chromosomal translocations commonly encountered in plasma cell myeloma other than MYC rearrangements have not been described in de novo PBL. EBV-negative PBL cases show a higher mutation load and more frequent TP53, CARD11, and MYC mutations, whereas EBV-positive PBLs tend to have more mutations affecting the JAK/STAT pathway {33951889}. Somatic mutations involving JAK/STAT, MAPK/ERK, and NOTCH pathways are frequently detected {33951889; 33225311; 32273478; 34465776} together with TP53 mutations (see #29254Table 4.35). The microRNA expression profile of PBL reveals a number of EBV-encoded microRNAs, suggesting a pathogenetic role of EBV-encoded microRNAs in the lymphomagenesis of EBV-positive cases {29296171}. Gene expression profiling has demonstrated downregulation of B-cell receptor signalling and upregulation of plasma cell differentiation–associated genes and MYC {25921246}.

PBL demonstrates a destructive infiltrate composed of large immunoblastic and plasmablastic cells. A starry-sky pattern and brisk mitotic activity may be identified. Intermediate-sized lymphoplasmacytoid cells and plasma cells constitute a minor component of the infiltrate in rare cases.

Immunohistochemistry

Immunohistochemistry demonstrates absent CD20 expression and reduced/absent expression of PAX5 and CD45 (LCA). CD79a is positive in 40% of cases. Expression of markers associated with plasma cell differentiation, such as CD138, CD38, VS38c, Blimp1, and XBP1, are found in most cases. IRF4 (MUM1) is always positive {9028965; 20418245; 27687004; 27175027}. Immunoglobulin light chain restriction is usually demonstrable by immunohistochemistry or by flow cytometry. MYC protein is often expressed. Significantly higher levels of MYC protein expression are found in cases with MYC translocation or amplification {32273478}. Ki-67 is usually positive in > 90% of cells {26055271; 27687004}. PDL1 overexpression {27175027; 32273478} and loss or aberrant expression of MHC class II have been demonstrated {22689685}. CD10, CD56, and CD30 are positive in 20–30% of cases, whereas BCL6 is rarely positive. EBV association is demonstrable in 60% of cases {34465776} and is more frequent in patients with HIV (82%). ALK and KSHV/HHV8 latency-associated nuclear antigen (LANA) are negative. Rare cases with aberrant weak to moderate cytoplasmic expression of CD3 have been reported {29327711}. Rarely (< 10%), aberrant cytokeratin expression warrants a differential diagnosis with (undifferentiated) carcinoma {33165992}.

Differential diagnosis

PBL shows morphological and phenotypical overlap with diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) NOS with immunoblastic morphology {20736456; 33165992}, DLBCL with partial plasmablastic phenotype {20418245}, EBV-positive DLBCL {32118627}, and MYC-and BCL2-rearranged large B-cell lymphomas with plasmablastic features transformed from follicular lymphoma. ALK-positive large B-cell lymphoma and extracavitary/solid primary effusion lymphoma should be excluded. Expression of CD20 and/or PAX5 favours DLBCL over PBL, whereas expression of XBP1, Blimp1, and CD138 supports a diagnosis of PBL. Plasmablastic transformation of plasma cell myeloma (PCM) is usually heralded by a previous diagnosis of PCM, the presence of CRAB clinical features (hypercalcaemia, renal insufficiency, anaemia, and bone lesions) {15578069; 25193957; 32118627}, and bone marrow infiltration by mature clonal plasma cells. Genetic features of PCM (e.g. typical translocations or mutation spectrum) favour plasmablastic transformation of PCM over de novo PBL. Rare cases of PBL in HIV-positive individuals may show overlapping clinical features with PCM {20348882}. However, the distinction may not be made unequivocally in all cases.
Cells are large and non-cohesive, with abundant basophilic cytoplasm and central to eccentric large vesicular nuclei with distinct single nucleoli.
Monoclonal IG rearrangements can be demonstrated in PBL.

Essential: lymphoma with plasmablastic/immunoblastic morphology; expression of plasma cell–associated antigens (e.g. IRF4 [MUM1], CD138, Blimp1); negativity for CD20, PAX5, ALK, and KSHV/HHV8.

Desirable: EBV positivity (EBV-encoded small RNA [EBER]) in about 60% of cases; detection of MYC rearrangements; detection of monoclonal IG rearrangements.
The Lugano system is used to stage lymphomas and has been adopted by the Union for International Cancer Control (UICC) TNM classification {25113753}.

The prognosis of PBL is poor, with a median overall survival time of 6–32 months with conventional chemotherapy. Patients diagnosed with low clinical stage have shown more favourable outcomes {26055271; 26795083}. A high International Prognostic Index (IPI) score and the presence of MYC translocations or gain have a negative impact on outcome {24832164}.
